summary: Defines a MIB module for modeling the CAPWAP protocol that controls and provisions wireless access points. It is a basis for future work on managing CAPWAP with SNMP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a list of dials and gauges for the boss that tells wifi boxes what to do.

questions: wireless access point central controller management
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing wireless access points controlled by a central controller.

tldr.problem: Wireless networks increasingly use a centralized controller to manage many access points, but management tools lack a standardized way to monitor and configure this setup via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines MIB objects for managing CAPWAP (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points), using the ifIndex mechanism to reuse existing wireless technology MIBs and create a unified management interface.
tldr.outcome: Operators can centrally manage wireless networks through SNMP using standard MIB objects, avoiding proprietary management interfaces.

today: RFC 5833 is an Informational document that serves as the foundation for SNMP management of CAPWAP-based wireless networks. It has not been obsoleted. Vendors implementing centralized wireless controllers often use these MIB definitions or extensions of them to provide management capabilities in their products.

sections.title: Centralized Wireless Network Management
sections.content:
The CAPWAP Protocol (RFC 5415) defines how an Access Controller (AC) manages a collection of Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). This RFC provides the SNMP management information base (MIB) to monitor and configure CAPWAP-based networks.

Unlike traditional autonomous wireless networks where each access point operates independently, centralized networks concentrate control functions on a central controller while WTPs handle only radio transmission and reception. This architecture simplifies deployment and configuration of large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of managing each wifi box separately, one central box talks to them all and tells them what to do.

sections.title: Design of the CAPWAP-BASE-MIB Module
sections.content:
The MIB module follows the CAPWAP centralized control model: the SNMP agent runs on the AC, not on WTPs. It is independent of any wireless technology, allowing reuse of existing IEEE 802.11, 802.16, and other vendor wireless binding MIBs.

A key design innovation is the use of WTP Virtual Radio Interfaces. Each physical radio on a WTP is represented by an ifIndex (interface index) on the AC, using the standard Interfaces MIB (IF-MIB). This allows operators to configure WTP radios through standard wireless technology MIBs as if the radios were locally connected to the AC, simplifying management.
sections.plainLanguage: The central controller pretends the wifi boxes' radios are connected to it directly, so managers can use the same tools they already know.

sections.title: Key MIB Tables
sections.content:
The MIB defines nine main tables. AC Name List Table: configures a list of AC names. MAC ACL Table: configures access control lists (ACLs) for stations. WTP Profile Table: configures WTP profiles (static configurations) before WTPs connect to the AC, including the WTP's Base MAC address and model number. WTP State Table: shows the AC's current state (Finite State Machine state) for each WTP. WTP Table: displays running WTP properties. Wireless Binding Table: maps WTP IDs and radio IDs to ifIndexes and wireless binding types.

Station Table provides information about connected wireless clients. WTP Events Stats Table and Radio Events Stats Table collect counters for reboots, failures, channel changes, and other events on WTPs and radios.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has tables for: wifi boxes before they connect, their current status, their addresses, the radios on them, the devices connected to them, and how many times things broke.

sections.title: Reusing Wireless Technology MIBs
sections.content:
A major design goal is to avoid reinventing management for specific wireless technologies. The RFC includes a mechanism to reuse MIB modules from other SDOs (such as IEEE). For example, the IEEE 802.11 MIB defines dot11OperationTable for configuring radio operation parameters. By using ifIndex mapping, the AC allows managers to configure a WTP's radios through these existing tables.

This approach means that a CAPWAP binding for a new wireless technology (like 802.16) needs only a minimal CAPWAP-specific MIB for technology-unique settings. The bulk of management can leverage existing MIBs, reducing implementation burden.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing brand-new management tables for each type of wifi, the CAPWAP MIB bridges to the existing official tables, so you do not have to learn new ones.

sections.title: WTP Profiles and Virtual Interfaces
sections.content:
A WTP profile is a pre-configuration used before a WTP connects to the AC. The profile must include the WTP's Base MAC address (the unique hardware identifier), which the AC uses to match the WTP to its profile when it connects. The profile also includes the WTP's model number, which defines how many physical radios the WTP has.

When a WTP profile is created with a model number, the AC automatically creates an equal number of WTP Virtual Radio Interfaces on itself. Each virtual radio gets an ifIndex, and the manager can then configure that radio's behavior through standard wireless technology MIBs, such as IEEE 802.11 tables, using the virtual radio's ifIndex.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a wifi box shows up, you create a profile saying 'when MAC address X arrives, it should have 2 radios', and the central box prepares 2 virtual radio slots for it.
